Colored Lad's Eyebrow Torn Off—Not a Scratch on Carmody, His Accuser.
Colored Lad's Eyebrow Torn Off—Not a Scratch on Carmody, His Accuser.

George W. Sewell, a colored boy of 18, who lives at 414 West Twenty-eighth street, was arraigned in the West Side court yesterday, charged with violating a corporation ordinance and assaulting the policeman who arrested him, Patrolman Patriok J. Carmody of the West Thirty-seventh street station. Sewell, who is a slender lad, presented a pitiable appearance. His eyebrow was torn loose, his head was out and his face was swollen to the size of a cocoanut. Incidentally, the cop hadn't a scratch on him.

According to Carmody's story, Sewell, with some other young colored boys, started a fire in the street in front of 406 West Twenty-eighth street. Carmody ordered them to put it out, displaying his shield. Sewell, he said, cursed him and knocked him down. The negro lad was too frightened to say anything and Magistrate Pool held him in $500 for examination to-day.

Carmody took him by the arm and started to haul him to the prison, when the boy broke loose and ran out into the court room crying, "Don't let him take me down there. He beat me last night. He's going to beat me again to-day."

"Of course he beat you—anybody can see that at a glance," said Magistrate Pool. "You will have a chance to tell your story to-morrow." Then he ordered another cop to take the boy back to the prison.

Sewell works for William H. Fowler of 415 West 115th street, trustee of the estate of John Cattnach, and manager of the Cattnach Trunk Manufactory at 50 West Thirty-fourth street. Fowler bailed the boy out and expressed great surprise at the charge against him.

"He has been in my employ for five years," said Mr. Fowler, "and he is a very obedient, polite and useful boy. He is not the least belligerent, and I cannot believe the charge against him."

After being bailed out Sewell seemed to regain some of his courage. He said that the charge of assault was wholly false.

"Some other boys and I were standing around a fire, though I didn't start it, when this man came up in citizen's clothes and told us to put out the fire. He didn't say he was a policeman or show a shield, but he hit me in the eye and then pounded me. It was only to save himself from the crowd that he finally threw back his coat and showed a shield."

Mr. Fowler said he believed the boy's story and would be on hand to-day to see that be got justice.

"Prisoner, you are discharged. Make a charge of felonious assault against this officer and I will hold him in $1,000 bail," said Magistrate Pool at the conclusion of the examination of George Sewell, the eighteen-year-old colored boy who says he was badly beaten by Policeman Carmody of the West Thirty-seventh street station on Sunday night.

"I ask for an adjournment, Judge, so that I can bring some witnesses, said Carmody.

"You cannot have any adjournment," replied the Magistrate. "This case has been up before me twice, and you have had ample time to produce all the witnesses you want. You would only go out and get manufactured testimony. Any police officer would give it for you," said Magistrate Pool. As Carmody walked from the bridge the Magistrate added: "Don't let that officer go. He is a prisoner under $1,000 bail."

The case, of which this was the dramatic end, first came before the court on Monday, when Sewell was arraigned by Carmody on the charge of violating a corporation ordinance and assaulting an officer. As the prisoner was being led back to his cell by Carmody he suddenly broke loose from the officer and ran back into the court room screaming, "Don't let him take me down there. He beat me yesterday and he will beat me again to-day." The prisoner's race, with torn eyebrow, cut scalp and swollen, discolored cheek suggested that there might be something in that, and Magistrate Pool ordered that the boy be taken to the prison by another policeman, promising that he would have an opportunity to tell his story.

The story told by Carmody, both at the preliminary hearing on Monday and at the examination yesterday, was that while walking through West Twenty-eighth street late on Sunday night he came across a mattress blazing in the street. He accused Sewell of starting the fire, and told him he was liable to arrest. Sewell knocked him into the gutter, he said, ruining his suit of clothes, and then, jumping on him started to thrash him. He struck the boy in self-defence twice with the butt of his revolver. The cop is several inches taller than the colored boy and probably weighs fifty pounds more.

Carmody admitted that he was in plain clothes, that he was off duty and that he was carrying his revolver.

"If you were off duty, why did you carry your revolver? Didn't you know that a policeman off duty has no right to carry concealed weapons?" asked the Magistrate. Carmody said he did not know it.

"Then you had better learn the rules of your department," said the Magistrate. "Did you show your shield?"

"I had no chance," replied Carmody. "The defendant knocked me down and jumped on me."

"Didn't you hit this boy because he was black?" asked the Magistrate. Carmody said he did not.

"Of course you did. There is no doubt of it," replied the Magistrate. "A man of your physical ability ought to be able to take care of a little fellow like this without a gun."

Sewell then testified that he was about to enter his home at 414 West Twenty-eighth street, when he stopped to look at a mattress that was blazing in the street. At the same moment Carmody came up to him and accused him of starting the fire. Sewell had no idea that Carmody, who was in plain clothes, was a policeman. Sewell answered, "You'll have to see the party who did set it afire. I don't know anything about it."

Just then, he said, Fred Ellis, who lives in the same house, came out and spoke to him, not seeing the policeman. "Well, what have you got to say about this?" Carmody said to Ellis. Ellis apologized for interrupting, whereupon Carmody pulled his revolver with an oath and stuck it in Ellis's face. At the sight of the gun Sewell ducked and ran, slipped and fell in the gutter and Carmody either fell or jumped on top of him, gun in hand. CARMODY'S RECORD. Policeman Charged With Assaulting Negro Has Been in Trouble Before.
Deputy Police Commissioner McAvoy would make no comment yesterday on the action of Magistrate Pool in holding Policeman Patrick Carmody on trial for assaulting a negro boy.

The police records show that Carmody has had thirty-four complaints against him since he was appointed a policeman on May 2, 1894, and has been fined an aggregate of fifty-eight and a half days pay. Eight times he has been charged with being absent from roll call. Seven times he was charged with being absent from post. Once he was fined five days pay for failing to properly patrol his post.

His last appearance at Police Headquarters was on the charge of being absent from a public school where he was supposed to be on duty.
george-sewell-new-york.A8:
POLICEMAN MAKES A RECORD. Thirty-four Complaints Against Patrick Carmody. Patrolman Patrick Carmody, of the West Thirty-seventh-street station, whom Magistrate Pool held in $1,000 bail for assaulting a negro prisoner, has had thirty-four complaints entered against him since his appointment to the force on May 2, 1894, and from the consequent trials penalties aggregating 58½ days' pay have been imposed by the different Police Judges presiding, says the New York Evening Post. Carmody's record up to date shows the following complaints figuring conspicuously: "Absent from roll-call," eight times; "absent from post," seven times. One entry indicates that he has been fined for being absent from his post without being relieved; several more that he had been repeatedly punished for loitering and "sitting during patrol." "Did not properly patrol" is the charge which is most frequent on his record, and on one occasion the patrolman was fined five days' pay for this offense. His last appearance before a trial judge was on May 5, this year, when a fine of three days' pay was imposed for his being "absent from public school." DANIEL COME TO JUDGMENT.
The courageous action of Judge Pool, magistrate in the 56th street court, in holding Policeman Connody as a prisoner charged with felonious assault and in sending him to the Tombs subject to indictment by the grand jury for brutally clubbing a young Afro-American, man, George Bewell, has been the sensation of the week in judicial and police circles and has aroused the public-spirited citizens of New York in defense of his action. One of the most dramatic scenes ever enacted in a meritorious court in this city occurred when Judge Pool, discharging Bewell, assured him that, instead of being a violator of the law, all of his civil rights an American citizen had been outrageously invaded by one who is supposed to be a protector of the citizens, and, when Officer Connody asked to have the case adjourned to enable him to get witnesses, replied: "You cannot have an adjournment. This case has been before me twice and if you had witnesses you have had plenty of time to get them. I will not allow you to manufacture evidence. Many police officers would give it for you to get you out of the consequences of your own outrageous act." After these remarks of conscience, Connody turned to leave the bridge, Magistrate Pool said to the court sergeant: "Halt that officer, he is a prisoner under $1,000 bail, whom I charge with felonious assault." The court officers, attorneys, witnesses and spectators, who make up the daily crowd, swayed by feelings of amazement which soon gave way to admiration at this unprecedented action of a magistrate. The facts brought out at the afternoon session were these: Near 25th street and 9th avenue a bonfire was started by some Italian children. JIM CHERRY BEATEN.
Negro Who Made Derogatory Remarks Had Narrow Escape.
Sulphur Springs, Tex., Aug. 12.—Jim Cherry, a yellow negro, made a derogatory statement concerning the character of Miss Nettle Griggs. He was beaten and a consultation held by citizens whether or not to lynch him. Finally he was ordered to leave town, which he did in a covered wagon.

ARRESTED FOR PEONAGE.
Five Planters Charged with Offence Against One Negro.
(By Telegraph to The Tribune.)
Aug. 25 — Elve Lafayette

Memphis, Aug. 25.—Five Lafayette County, Miss., planters, charged with peonage, have been arrested by the federal authorities in that State. The five offences were committed on one negro, whom the white men seem to have held and worked by turns. Three of the planters are wealthy brothers, owning a sawmill, as well as plantations. They worked the negro in the mill and farms, turning him over, it is said, to the other two, when they needed him. It is alleged that they said they were holding and working the man for debts due the five. This is the first case in that section.

FIVE MEN ARRESTED FOR ALLEGED PEONAGE
Special to The Light.

Oxford, Miss., Aug. 26.—Brigham Young, Allen Young, James Young, Lee Rogers, and Charles Butts, white, were arrested in the southwestern part of this city by federal authorities, charged with peonage.

It is claimed they held John Ross, a negro, in bondage and otherwise restrained him of his liberty.

The Younys are well-to-do people and own a large farm and saw mill near the scene which they were arrested.

They all gave bond for their appearance before United States Commissioner Oldham Tuesday, September 5.

This is the first case of the kind ever reported in this country.

The Negroes of Knoxville, Tenn., have refused to ride on the street cars on the majority of the lines during the past few days, and the white people have the cars to themselves. The trouble first started on the Lousdale Line after the "Jim Crow" law went into effect, by a mob tearing the Negroes off the cars. Since then, and after the officers took a hand, a number of colored mollers and other laborers employed at large industries, have been circulating among the colored people creating an impression and sentiment against riding on cars with the result that the colored people have not only formed an organization with the intention of boycotting the street cars on account of the Jim Crow law, but on two lines they have started hacks running. They have gone about it quietly and without any demonstration.

NEGRO BOYCOTT

IS AFFECTING THE TENNESSEE STREET RAILWAYS.

FEELING IS VERY BITTER

Against the Companies, Which They Believe Had "Jim Crow"
Law Passed.

Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 8.—[Special.]—The street railways in Nashville, Memphis, Chattanooga, and Knoxville are wrestling with the separate-seat law, by which the races must be separated in the cars and which was enacted at the last session of the Legislature. Maj. Warner, of the Chattanooga street railway, says the receipts of his line have been cut from 8 to 10 per cent. because of the boycott instituted by the negroes. There has also been a marked falling off in negro passengers in Memphis and Nashville. Knoxville has not suffered so much because its negro population is small.

The negroes who live at a distance from their work in Nashville are being hauled to and fro in wagons which go to their homes early in the morning and meet them at their places of employment in the evening. Most of the negroes, however, are walking. They are very bitter against the car companies, most of them being advised that the car companies had the law passed to keep them from riding.

The negro leaders in Memphis and Nashville are raising funds with which to test the constitutionality of the law. Memphis negroes have a fund of $5,000 about subscribed.

The boycott is undoubtedly affecting the receipts of all the companies.

Every day makes it evident that nothing great and exalting engages the southern mind. The tendency of the dominant thought is self-aggravization and a hardened discrimination against the poor blacks of God-suffering humanity. Not content with the oppression of more than three centuries imposed upon Afro-Americans, the southern people persistently and defiantly perseis this race against all the holy provisions touchsafed by national law for the equal care and protection of all citizens alike. Instead of elevating they seek to degrade, and when admonished of their crimes, they declare themselves to be the best friends known to our people of the south. In the days of our bondage they professed even as much, while with unrelenting hand they persecuted and tortured without mercy. We need hardly wonder now that the same spirit of oppression still characterizes the southern mind. We have every reason to expect better things of the southern people, for they have shown themselves brave and courageous in countless ways. WOMAN ASSAULTED BY BLACK BRUTE
Georgia Mob Hunting For Perpetrator of Crime.
LYNCHING IS VERY PROBABLE
He Had Been Working on Woman's Husband on Farm—Whole Community Is Aroused Over the Awful Crime.
Husband on Farm—Whole Community Is Aroused Over the Awful Crime.

Thomasville, Ga., August 17.—This morning at 7 o'clock a negro, Manuel Harty by name, assaulted Mrs. Chas. Outze, wife of a young farmer living 3 miles south of town, and made his escape.

The negro was a Thomasville man, and had worked for Outze only two days. Mr. Outze was boiling sirup half a mile from his home. The negro went to his residence and asked for a key to the cotton house, saying he had left his coat there. Mrs. Outze handed him the key, and as she did so, he caught hold of her and choking her he accomplished his purpose.

The negro then stole a pistol and a shotgun from the kitchen and ran off through the wods.

Alarmed by his wife's screams Outze ran to the house to find her in a desperate condition. He was in time to see the fleeing negro, but could not overtake him.

Outze then rode to Thomasville at breakneck speed for medical aid and to inform the officers of law.

NEGRO MURDERER KILLED BY POSSE
Associated Press.

Birmingham, Ala., Aug. 23.—A special to the News from Selma, Ala., says two white men and a negro have been killed and another white man was wounded in two shooting affairs at Tunnell Springs.

Oliver Lott, a negro laborer at the lumber mill of G. Talley, had left the mill owing to a debt to John, and Harry Helton, two carpenters and brothers.

In a discussion with the Helton brothers Lott opened fire on them, killing John Helton and seriously wounding Harry Helton.

The negro then fled and barricaded himself in a house.

A posse of citizens under the leadership of G. Talley attempted to arrest him and surrounded the house, but Lott refused to surrender and opened fire on the crowd.

Talley was mortally wounded and died a few hours later.

The posse then fired on the negro's house and his body was afterwards found riddled with bullets.

Negro Barricades Himself After Shooting Two Men
CITIZENS CAPTURE SLAYER
But Not Until After His Body Had Been Riddled With Bullets—Tragedy Occurred at Tunnel Springs.
Selma, August 23.—(Special.)—Information reached Selma today of a desperate encounter at Tunnel Springs on the Pensacola division of the Louisville and Nashville road about sixty-two miles south of Selma. The affair took place yesterday morning and the result is as follows:

The Dead.

John Helton.
G. Tally.
Oliver Lett, colored.

The Wounded.

Harry Helton.
Unknown negro.

The two Heltons are employed by G. Tally, who runs a mill at Tunnel Springs. Lett had also been employed by Mr. Tally but had quit work indebted to his employer. Yesterday morning the two Heltons went to Lett's house and told him to come to work. He refused to go at first and he was then asked to pay what he owed. The negro is said to have then agreed to go to see Mr. Tally and the two men started out of the house, when Lett seized his Winchester and fired twice. The first ball struck John Helton, killing him. The second wounded his brother Harry.

Barricades Himself In House.

Lett then left the house and went to the home of another negro and barricaded himself in the house. The owner of the house was compelled to stay in the house with him. News of the killing soon spread and a posse was formed to capture the negro. Mr. Tally and a Mr. Farrlor drove within range of the house which was being surrounded by the posse and the horse becoming restless Mr. Tally got out and went to his head. While standing on the ground a shot came from the house and struck Mr. Tally in the neck. The wound was not considered serious until last night, when an attempt was made to get a physician from this city, but there was no train until this morning, when Dr. J. P. Furniss went down on the Louisville and Nashville pay car, which was enroute to Pensacola. About 10 o'clock this morning, shortly after the arrival of the physician, Mr. Tally died.

Fire Shots at House.

The citizens of the community then determined to capture the negro dead or alive and a hundred shots were fired into the house. One of these struck the innocent negro, whose house had been taken charge of by the slayer of the Heltons and Mr. Tally. His name was not learned but he managed to escape further injury and made his way to a doctor.

Lett was finally captured, that is his body was found full of holes, either one of which would have caused his instant death.

Mr. Tally is quite a well-known citizen of his community. He was in Selma a few weeks ago in an infirmary under treatment for pleurisy and had only late-ly gone back to his home.

TWO WHITE MEN KILLED
DEADLY WORK OF BAD NEGRO'S REVOLVER.
Tragedy Occurred at Tunnell Springs Saw Mill and Murderer Wna Killed After Long and Desperate Struggle.
Advertiser Bureau.
Salma. Aug. 28

The details of a shooting scrape which took place at a place called Tunnel Springs, about sixty miles south of this city on the Pensacola division of the Louisville & Nashville Railroad, was learned here this morning. The shooting resulted in the death of two white men and a negro and the serious wounding of another man who it is thought will not recover from the wound that he received from the pistol in the hands of the negro.

The shooting Rook place at the saw mill owned by G. Tally and which is near Tunnel Springs and about two miles from Beatrice. The information regarding the shooting as learned here is meagre but the facts relating to the tragedy which is greatly deplored by the citizens of that community is as follows:

There is employed at the saw mill of G. Tally two white carpenters, whose names are John Helton and Harry Helton. Up to a few days ago there has been also employed at the mill a negro by the name of Oliver Lett. The negro overdrew his salary a few days ago and since then has not been near the saw mill to work. Sometimes yesterday the two brothers met him and got after him for his not coming back to work after having been paid for it.

In the conversation that ensued between the men the negro got mad and used some very abusive language and a fight started between them. The negro pulled a pistol and began shooting. He first shot at John Helton and the ball lodged in that young man's breast and he died shortly afterwards. The other brother was not armed and started to defend himself as best he could when the negro turned and shot him the ball entering his side and inflicting a painful and serious wound which may prove fatal.

After shooting the two men Lett left the place where the shooting occurred and went to his home which was close by. When he arrived there he barricaded himself in the house. After the shooting of the two brothers Mr. Tally got together a number of citizens of that place and went to the home of the negro to arrest him for the murder of John Helton. When they found that Lett had barricaded himself in the house they tried to get him to come out and surrender. But this the negro would not do and opened fire on the crowd with his pistol.

A shot struck Mr. Tally in the neck inflicting a serious wound from which he died at his home near where the shooting occurred at 10 o'clock this morning. After Tally had been shot the posse of citizens began shooting at the house in which the negro was. The house was a very flimsy one and the shots from the guns and pistols penetrated the walls. Finally when no answering shots came from the house the door was broken in and the negro was found lying dead on the floor his body having been riddled with bullets that had plowed their way through the walls of the house. An effort was made late last night to run a special train from this city to Tunnel Springs to carry Dr. Furniss there so that Mr. Tally could have medical attention, but the road was unable to send out a special. This morning Dr. Furniss went down on

It is stated that the shooting caused considerable excitement around Tunnel Springs and that that there was considerable fear fear felt for many many of the negroes of that neighborhood, but today everything is reported to have quieted down and it is now thought that there there will be no more trouble.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN ALABAMA.
Desperate Negro Kills Three Men and Is Shot to Death.
Selma, Ala., August 24.—News has just been received of a wholesale killing that took place at Tunnell Springs, a small station on the Louisville and Nashville railroad between Selma and Flomaton yesterday.

The particular as they could be obtained at this writing, are that a negro named Oliver Lott owed C. Talley a bill, which he had placed in the hands of John and Harry Helton, who were carpenters in the employ of Talley for collection. In trying to force a collection of the debt, a dispute arose and the negro, who was armed, shot and killed John Holton and wounded the other Holton, making his escape. He was soon afterwards pursued by armed men, and when cornered in a house, pulled his gun and shot G. Tally. Tally lingered until 10 o'clock this morning when he died.

Medical aid was summoned from Selma but the wound proved fatal.

The negro Lott was shot to pieces in the house, his body being literally filled with lead.
